items.text: Zakaj nista šla k marmalni hiši?
items.q: Ghassem, a boy, reuses the mispronounced word for marble that Maman used earlier. Does 'marmalni hiši' read as that same slip?
before: …kolo se je vrtelo. Bilo je rdeče. Kot tista velika rdeča vrata. Sedel sem ob jarku. Noge sem položil v jarek. Vode ni bilo. Srce sem imel prazno. Moški se je vrnil. Sprednje kolo se ni več vrtelo. Omidu je dal klofuto. Oba sva jokala. Moški je odšel. Ghassem se je vrnil. Grajal nas je. Rekel je:

items.text: Tako pač govorim. Vi mislite, da recitujem pesmi.
items.q: Hamid, a boy, answers in the rhythm and rhyme of his own poems. Does this line sound like a playful rhyme?
before: Hamid je rekel v istem ritmu, s katerim je recitiral svoje pesmi:

items.text: Kdor hoče imeti brezpotrebno filozofsko razpravo, lahko gre v kuhinjo.
items.q: Hooman crudely tells his roommates to take their philosophical bullshit to the kitchen. Does this sound as crude as he would say it?
before: Eskandar in Meysam sta začela analizirati, kako je tisto, kar se je zgodilo na Fakulteti za strojništvo, kaplja, ki pokaže morje. Povezala sta to s konkurenčnim, potrošniškim svetom danes in takimi stvarmi. Njuna razprava se je zavlekla. Hooman je ugasnil luč in rekel:

items.text: Po tisti zgodbi z lokalizacijo se ne bom čudil ničemur, kar nam pade na glavo.
items.q: Hooman means that after that policy, whatever prick lands on their heads won't surprise him. Does this sound as crude as his usual talk?
before: Bahman je rekel, da ni problema. Eskandar je segel z roko pod mojo posteljo, da bi izvlekel knjigo, Meysam pa je klečal in razgrinjal svoje ležišče pod obešalnikom. Hooman ju je opazoval in rekel:

items.text: Požiralec tičjih glav, zakaj kvasiš neumnosti?
items.q: Hooman hurls a crude insult at a roommate who is talking nonsense. Does 'Požiralec tičjih glav' sound like a real insult?

items.text: Ne jej žalosti, moj pametni deček.
items.q: Maman comforts her little boy, whose feet are hurt. A Persian expression kept word for word: can you guess its meaning?

items.text: Pravim, da če samo sediš tu in bereš poezijo, se ti nobena voda ne bo segrela.
items.q: A friend criticises Amir for reading poetry all day. A Persian expression kept word for word: can you guess its meaning?

items.text: Haha, Starešina Krčme, Stari – odlično. Zadel si, Leopard Farid.
items.q: Hooman shortens the nickname 'Starešina Krčme' to a pet form. Does 'Stari' work as that short nickname?
before: Hooman je s pisalom pisal kaj v knjigo in rekel:

items.text: Potem samo pomisli, kaj mora naš ubogi Baba preživeti – vsa ta leta brez dela doma.
items.q: Ghassem, holding back a laugh, mocks their idle father with fake pity. Does this sentence read correctly?
before: Ghassem reče z glasom, iz katerega čutiš pridržan smeh:

items.text: Kur te, sto sedemdeset metrov si me s to postavo vlekel za seboj.
items.q: Hooman, panting, curses Amir for making him chase him so far. Does 'Kur te' sound natural as a curse?
before: – Še če upoštevamo tisti zadnji del, ki postane ožji in gre skoraj do vrat Valiasr, postane sto sedemdeset metrov.

items.text: Po nekaj časa je začel objavljati objave o propadanju sodobnega človeka zaradi družbenih omrežij
items.q: Hooman says that after a while the guy began posting about the decline of modern man. Does this read correctly?
before: – ... celo enkrat mi je poslal zasebno sporočilo in vprašal, ali bi bil tako prijazen, da mu ne všečkam objav. Jaz pa sem mu odgovoril z velikanskim emotikonom palca gor, haha.

items.text: Kodrasti, zvenite tako presenečeni, kot da ste prišli na univerzo brez Konkoorja.
items.q: Hooman mocks one curly-haired roommate for acting surprised. Does this sound like how a young man would talk to him?

items.text: Preklet bodi, kdor zanika Orlov Pogled News.
items.q: Farid mock-solemnly curses anyone who doubts Sajad, the room's gossip source, nicknamed Eagle Eye News. Does this sound playful?

items.text: Puf, ampak prekleto, spakiral si se in odšel tja, zdaj pa sediš in se smejiš naši bradi in našemu kurcu.
items.q: Hooman teases Amir crudely for leaving Iran and laughing at the friends left behind. Does this sound natural?
